title: Sister Steel #1: Tempered
author: Ilse Marek
blurb: A foundry hand walks into a management office to ask where her brother went, and does not leave until somebody tells her. Written, drawn, lettered and inked by one woman over fourteen months, printed on paper so coarse you can feel the grain through the sleeve. Banned in two districts, which sold it in the other eighteen.
source: Scanned from the Mint Condition reading copy, Ironside Street, Coldwater. In-universe fiction.

chapters.title: Chapter One — Heat
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. Full bleed. The pour.

A ladle the size of a car tipping white metal into a mould, and the white is the white of the paper — Marek never drew light, she drew the absence of ink around it, and on this page the whole top half is bare newsprint and it still burns your eyes at arm's length.

Silhouetted against it, six figures in leathers, all identical at this distance, all doing their jobs.

CAPTION: Number Four Foundry ran three shifts and had done since before the sky changed. The metal did not care what year it was and neither, in the end, did anybody who worked it.

PANEL TWO. Ground level. A woman lifting her visor. Face wet, hair flattened, a burn scar down one forearm shaped like a run of solder. This is Marta. Marek drew her from the mirror and never admitted it.

MARTA: Where's Tobin.

PANEL THREE. A man shrugs, not unkindly, already turning back to the work.

MAN: Office wanted him.

MARTA: Office wanted him when.

MAN: Start of shift.

PANEL FOUR. Close on Marta. Nothing on her face at all.

CAPTION: It was the end of shift.

PAGE TWO.

PANEL ONE. The walk. Marek's famous nine-panel grid, and in every panel Marta is the same size in the same place, and only the corridor changes behind her — the shop floor, the wash, the yard, the covered way, the stairs, the carpet, the good carpet, the reception, the door.

No dialogue. Nine panels, no dialogue. It takes eleven seconds to read and it is the most quoted page in Coldwater comics.

PANEL TEN, breaking the grid, bleeding off the right edge: her hand on the office door handle, and the handle is brass, and it is the only clean object she has touched all day.

PAGE THREE.

PANEL ONE. The office. Carpet, a desk, a window with a blind half down, and behind the desk a man who stands up when she comes in — Marek is careful about this. He stands up. He is polite. He is polite for the entire book.

FOREMAN: Marta. You can't be in here in those.

MARTA: Where's my brother.

FOREMAN: Sit down.

MARTA: Where's my brother.

PANEL TWO. He sits back down himself, which is worse.

FOREMAN: Tobin's been reassigned.

PANEL THREE. Silence panel. Just the blind, and the light through it, ruled across the carpet in bars.

PANEL FOUR.

MARTA: To where.

FOREMAN: I genuinely don't know. That's not me being careful with you. There's a form, it goes up, it doesn't come back. I sign it and it's gone.

PANEL FIVE. Close on his hands. They are clean and they are shaking very slightly, and Marek renders that with three short repeated lines at the knuckle, and it is the whole man in three lines.

FOREMAN: Sixty this year.

MARTA: Sixty.

FOREMAN: Sixty-one, with him.

PANEL SIX. She has not moved.

FOREMAN: I have asked. I want you to know I have asked.

MARTA: What did they say.

FOREMAN: They said the foundry's throughput is up.

PAGE FOUR.

PANEL ONE. Wide, low. Marta from the foreman's eyeline, standing in his office in her leathers with the light behind her, and the composition is exactly the cover, and this is the moment the cover is drawn from — which readers do not notice until the second reading, because on the cover she is holding a length of rebar, and here her hands are empty.

MARTA: Give me the form.

FOREMAN: There isn't a copy.

MARTA: Give me the one you signed.

FOREMAN: Marta —

MARTA: You said you sign it. So you had it in your hand. So you read a name and a number and a place, and you are going to give me the place.

PANEL TWO. He looks at the blind.

PANEL THREE. He looks at the blind.

PANEL FOUR. He tells her.

We do not get the word. Marek draws the speech balloon and leaves it empty — no ellipsis, no scratched-out lettering, just white — and for eighty years people have said this was a printing fault and for eighty years the people who know have said it was not.

chapters.title: Chapter Two — The Gate
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. Night, and a road out of the district that Marek drew from life, so that everyone who has walked it recognises the third telegraph pole.

Marta walking. Still in leathers. Carrying nothing.

CAPTION: She did not go home first. People have made a great deal of this. She did not go home first because home was two streets the wrong way and she was already walking, and that is all it was, and every reprint's introduction gets this wrong.

PANEL TWO. A gate. Chain-link, three metres, wire along the top, and beyond it a yard of nothing much: sheds, a hardstand, a lit window.

PANEL THREE. A guard hut. A man inside with the small blue light of a screen on his face.

MARTA: I'm here for Tobin Vey.

GUARD: There's no —

MARTA: I know there's no. I'm here anyway.

PANEL FOUR. He looks at her properly for the first time. Marek gives him a real face: young, bored, cold, not a monster, wearing a coat that doesn't fit.

GUARD: Go home.

MARTA: What is this place.

GUARD: Go home.

MARTA: You don't know either.

PANEL FIVE. He doesn't answer, and the not-answering is drawn as him going back to the screen, and the blue light coming back up on his face.

PAGE SIX.

PANEL ONE. She sits down against the fence.

PANEL TWO. She is still sitting against the fence. The light in the hut has changed colour, so it is later.

PANEL THREE. Still sitting. Frost on the wire.

PANEL FOUR. Still sitting. Dawn coming up behind the sheds, which Marek draws with the same bare-paper trick as the pour, so that the sunrise and the molten metal are literally the same mark on the page.

CAPTION: She sat at that gate for nine days. Everything you have heard about what she did on the tenth is somebody's uncle's version. Here is what she did.

PAGE SEVEN.

PANEL ONE. A truck at the gate. Sheeted flatbed, ordinary.

PANEL TWO. She stands up. Nine days of stiff, and Marek draws the stiff — the hand on the fence, the slow unfolding, the second where the knee doesn't take it.

PANEL THREE. She walks to the middle of the road.

PANEL FOUR. She stands in the middle of the road.

PANEL FIVE. Wide: the truck, the gate, the guard hut, the woman in the road. Held. A lot of empty asphalt.

PAGE EIGHT.

PANEL ONE. The truck's horn. Rendered as a solid black shape crossing three panel borders, which was a thing nobody was doing in 2041 and which every foundry-district comic did for the next decade.

PANEL TWO. She does not move.

PANEL THREE. The driver's window comes down. He is fifty, he is tired, he has a flask on the dash.

DRIVER: I don't want this.

MARTA: Neither do I.

DRIVER: I've got a run.

MARTA: I've got a brother.

PANEL FOUR. He looks at the gate. He looks at the guard hut. He looks at the flask.

PANEL FIVE. He turns the engine off.

PAGE NINE.

PANEL ONE. The guard is out of the hut.

PANEL TWO. The guard is on the phone.

PANEL THREE. Another truck arrives behind the first, and stops, because the first one has stopped.

PANEL FOUR. Another.

PANEL FIVE. Another.

PANEL SIX. Full page. The road out of Number Four, drawn from above, from the height of the water tower — and it is trucks, all the way back to the district, all of them stopped, all of them with their engines off, and one woman standing in the middle of the road at the top of the frame, and she is about four millimetres tall.

CAPTION: Throughput, that week, was not up.

chapters.title: Chapter Three — Tempered
chapters.text:
PANEL ONE. An office. Not the foreman's — a better one, high up, with a window that has a view and a carpet that has never had a boot on it.

Two men and a woman on one side of a table. Marta on the other, still in the leathers, nine days of gate on her.

CAPTION: They brought her inside, in the end, because a woman standing in a road is a photograph and a woman sitting at a table is a negotiation, and they had people whose whole job was knowing the difference.

PANEL TWO.

EXECUTIVE: We can find your brother.

MARTA: Then find him.

EXECUTIVE: I said we can. I didn't say we would like to, and I didn't say it was free.

PANEL THREE. She waits.

EXECUTIVE: You go back to your shift. The road clears. The road clears today, and it clears because you cleared it, and people see you clear it. And in a week, quietly, without a photograph, your brother comes home.

PANEL FOUR. Close on Marta. Marek does the four-millimetre shoulder drop here too, which is either homage or theft depending on which of the two artists you drink with.

MARTA: And the other sixty.

EXECUTIVE: I'm sorry?

MARTA: Sixty this year. He said sixty. Sixty-one with mine.

PANEL FIVE. The executive's face does not change at all, and Marek draws it not changing across four consecutive identical panels, which on cheap paper looks like a printing error and is the single cruellest thing in the book.

PAGE ELEVEN.

PANEL ONE.

EXECUTIVE: One.

MARTA: Sixty-one.

EXECUTIVE: One. That is the offer. It is a very good offer and it is the only one, and I would like you to understand that I am not being cruel, I am being accurate. I can produce one man. I cannot produce sixty. Nobody in this building can produce sixty. You are asking me for a thing that does not exist and refusing a thing that does.

PANEL TWO. Silence.

PANEL THREE. Silence.

PANEL FOUR. Marta stands up.

PAGE TWELVE.

PANEL ONE. The corridor. The nine-panel grid again, in reverse — the good carpet, the carpet, the stairs, the covered way, the yard, the wash, the shop floor. Same size, same place, every panel.

In the eighth panel she picks up a length of rebar from a stack by the wall, without breaking stride, and Marek does not draw attention to it in any way. No close-up. No angle change. It is just in her hand in panel eight and it was not in panel seven.

PANEL NINE: the doorway to the pour, the white of the paper coming up behind her.

PAGE THIRTEEN.

Full page, no panel, no border. The cover image, at last, for real: Marta in the doorway of the foundry with the light behind her and the rebar held down at her side like a staff.

And below it, small, bottom right, in her own hand-lettering because Marek lettered everything herself:

SHE WAS SOMEBODY'S SISTER FIRST.
SHE WAS SIXTY-ONE PEOPLE'S SISTER BY FRIDAY.

CONTINUED

—

[Inside back cover, first printing only, removed from every subsequent edition:]

I worked Number Four for six years and my brother is not coming home and I am not going to pretend at the end of this that he is. If you have bought this you have given me eight credits and I have given you the truth with a woman drawn over the top of it so you would pick it up. I am sorry about that. It was the only way I could think of.

— I. M.
